title: Hittites
wiki_lead:
The Hittites () were an Anatolian Indo-European people who formed one of the first major civilizations of the Bronze Age in West Asia. The Hittite's ancestors migrated from the Proto-Indo-European homeland in the Pontic–Caspian steppe, arriving in central Anatolia some time before 2000 BC. They formed a succession of polities including Kussara (before 1750 BC), the Kanesh or Neša (c. 1750–1650 BC), and then an empire with its capital at Hattusa. The Hittite Empire reached its peak in the mid-14th century BC, encompassing most of Anatolia and parts of northern Syria and Upper Mesopotamia, and bordering the rival empires of the Hurri-Mitanni and Assyrians. 
From the 15th to 13th centuries BC, the Hittites were a major power of the Near East, coming into conflict with the New Kingdom of Egypt, the Middle Assyrian Empire, and the empire of Mitanni. By the 12th century, much of the Hittite Empire had been annexed by the Middle Assyrian Empire. In the aftermath of the Late Bronze Age collapse at the end of the 12th century, the Hittites splintered into several small independent states; some of these survived into the 8th century BC before being absorbed into the Neo-Assyrian Empire. Lacking a unifying continuity, their descendants scattered and ultimately merged into the modern populations of the Levant and Mesopotamia.
The Hittite language belongs to the Anatolian branch of the Indo-European language family; it and the closely-related Luwian language are the oldest historically attested Indo-European languages.

Etymology
The Hittites called their kingdom Hattusa (Hatti in Akkadian), a name received from the Hattians, an earlier people who had inhabited and ruled the central Anatolian region until the beginning of the second millennium BC, and who spoke an unrelated language known as Hattic. The modern conventional name "Hittites" is due to the initial identification of the people of Hattusa with the Biblical Hittites by 19th-century archaeologists, a view that has since come under greater academic scrutiny. The Hittites would have called themselves something closer to "Neshites" or "Neshians" after the city of Nesha, which flourished for some two hundred years until a king named Labarna renamed himself Hattusili I (meaning "the man of Hattusa") sometime around 1650 BC and established his capital city at Hattusa.


Modern discovery
French scholar Charles Texier was the first modern investigator to encounter Hittite ruins, in 1834, near the village of Boğazköy in modern Turkey. Texier found what he described as "a city as big as Athens in its golden age".  He wrote of finding a wall with two massive doors, one with a low relief representing a human form and  another door decorated with stone lions. This was Hattusa, the Hittite capital. Texier was not aware of what he had uncovered; he was seeking the ruins of ancient Tavium on the shore of the old Halys River (Kızılırmak River) in modern Turkey.

The earliest written attestation of the Hittites is in tablets found at the karum of Kanesh (now called Kültepe) which contain accounting records between Assyrian merchants and a "land of Hatti". Some names in the tablets were neither Hattic nor Assyrian, but clearly Indo-European.
The script on a monument at Boğazkale by a "People of Hattusas" discovered by William Wright in 1884 was found to match peculiar hieroglyphic scripts from Aleppo and Hama in Northern Syria. In 1887, excavations at Amarna in Egypt uncovered the diplomatic correspondence of Pharaoh Amenhotep III and his son, Akhenaten. Two of the letters from a "kingdom of Kheta"—apparently located in the same general region as the Mesopotamian references to "land of Hatti"—were written in standard Akkadian cuneiform, but in an unknown language.

They spoke Nesite, the earliest attested Indo-European language, recorded using cuneiform script adapted from Akkadian models, with tens of thousands of clay tablets recovered from Hattusa providing primary evidence of their administration, laws, and diplomacy. At its peak around 1300 BCE under kings like Suppiluliuma I, the empire controlled much of Anatolia, northern Syria, and parts of Upper Mesopotamia, rivaling Egypt and Assyria through military campaigns and vassal treaties. Key achievements included pioneering iron smelting around 1400 BCE for weapons and tools, granting tactical edges in warfare, and the Battle of Kadesh in 1274 BCE against Ramesses II, which culminated in the first documented peace treaty in 1258 BCE, preserved in cuneiform and hieroglyphic versions. Their legal codes emphasized restitution over retribution, influencing subsequent Near Eastern jurisprudence, while their polytheistic religion featured over a thousand deities, with the storm god Tarhunna prominent in rituals documented on tablets. The empire's sudden collapse circa 1200 BCE, marked by the abandonment of Hattusa, aligned with a rare three-year megadrought (1198â1196 BCE) inferred from tree-ring widths and carbon isotope ratios in Anatolian juniper samples, exacerbating famine in the semi-arid region and weakening defenses against Sea Peoples incursions. Remnants persisted as Neo-Hittite states in Syria and southeastern Anatolia until Assyrian conquests in the 8th century BCE.
